front: What is a finite probability space?
back: A finite set Omega of outcomes with weights p(omega) > 0 that sum to 1 (Section 1).

front: What is a random variable on a finite probability space?
back: A function X from Omega to the real numbers (Definition 1.1).

front: What is the distribution of a random variable X?
back: The map x to P(X = x), the sum of p(omega) over the outcomes with X(omega) = x (Definition 1.2).

front: What is the distribution function of X?
back: F(x) = P(X <= x) for real x (Definition 2.1).

front: What is the shape of the distribution function of a finite law?
back: Hypotheses: positive weights and distinct values x_1 to x_m in increasing order. Then F(x) = 0 for x < x_1 and F(x) = 1 for x >= x_m (Proposition 2.2(a)).

front: By how much does the distribution function of a finite law jump at a value x_k?
back: Hypotheses: positive weights and distinct values. The jump at x_k is p_k > 0, so F(x_k) minus the left limit at x_k equals p_k (Proposition 2.2(d)).

front: What is the quantile function of X?
back: For 0 < p <= 1, Q(p) = inf{x in R : F(x) >= p} (Definition 3.1), the left-endpoint convention.

front: What is Q(p) for a finite law with distinct values x_1 to x_m in increasing order?
back: Hypotheses: positive weights, distinct values, 0 < p <= 1. Q(p) = x_(k*), where k* is the least index k with F_k >= p. The index exists because F_m = 1 >= p (Proposition 3.2).

front: For a finite law with positive weights and distinct values, what is Q(p) when F_(k-1) < p <= F_k?
back: Hypotheses: positive weights and distinct values. Q(p) = x_k, with F_0 = 0 and 1 <= k <= m (Remark 3.3). At p = F_k this gives Q(F_k) = x_k, not x_(k+1).

front: What is the quantile of n equally likely distinct values?
back: Hypotheses: distinct values y_1 to y_n in increasing order, each with probability 1/n, and 0 < p <= 1. Then Q(p) = y_(ceil(pn)), the ceil(pn)-th smallest value, where ceil(pn) is the least integer at least pn (Proposition 3.4).

front: Which index is the 99% quantile of 200 equally likely distinct losses?
back: 198. Here pn = 198 is an integer, so the index is 198 (Example 3.5).

front: For the table of Example 3.6, what is Q(1/2)?
Is F(Q(p)) = p always true?
back: Hypotheses: finite law with positive weights and distinct values, and 0 < p <= 1. No. Proposition 3.2 gives F(Q(p)) >= p, not equality. In Example 3.6, Q(1/2) = 0, but F(0) = 3/5, not 1/2.

front: Is the 0.99 quantile of 150 equally likely distinct values the 148th smallest, because pn = 148.5 rounds down?
back: No. Hypotheses: n equally likely distinct values, 0 < p <= 1. The index is the least integer at least pn, so Proposition 3.4 gives ceil(148.5) = 149, not the floor, 148.

front: Does the grid check of Lab 1 prove Proposition 3.2 for every p?
back: No. Lab 1 compares the two forms of Q at 100 grid points p = j/100 for one table. The proof of Proposition 3.2 covers every p in (0, 1].

front: What is the expectation of a random variable with distinct values x_1 to x_m?
back: E[X] = sum over k of x_k p_k, where p_k = P(X = x_k) (Definition 1.1). It is the probability-weighted average of the values of X.

front: Does summing X(omega) p(omega) over outcomes give the same expectation?
back: Hypothesis: finite probability space with positive weights. Yes. The sum over outcomes of X(omega) p(omega) equals the sum over values of x_k p_k (Proposition 1.2), because the events {X = x_k} partition the outcome set.

front: Is expectation linear on a finite probability space?
back: Yes. For random variables U and V on the same finite probability space and constants alpha, beta, delta, E[alpha U + beta V + delta] = alpha E[U] + beta E[V] + delta (Proposition 1.3).

front: How is the expectation of a random variable with a continuous density f defined?
back: E[X] = integral of x f(x) dx over the real line, when the integral of |x| f(x) dx is finite (Definition 1.6).

front: What is the variance of X?
back: Var(X) = E[(X - mu)^2] with mu = E[X] (Definition 2.1). A variance is never negative, because it is the expectation of a square.

front: What is the shortcut formula for variance?
back: Hypotheses: finite probability space with positive weights. Var(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2 (Proposition 2.2).

front: Does scaling X by a constant a multiply its variance by a?
back: No. Hypothesis: finite probability space with positive weights. Var(aX + b) = a^2 Var(X) for constants a and b, so scaling multiplies the variance by a^2, and a shift b leaves it unchanged (Proposition 2.3).

front: When is the variance of a finite law zero?
back: Hypotheses: finite probability space with positive weights. Var(X) = 0 if and only if X takes exactly one value (Proposition 2.4).

front: What is E[X] for a fair six-sided die?
back: E[X] = 7/2 (Example 1.4): the average of the faces 1 to 6, each with probability 1/6.

front: What is the expectation of the two-point loss of Example 1.5, in cents?
back: E[L] = 12500 cents (Example 1.5).

front: Is the expectation always one of the values the variable takes?
back: No. For a fair die E[X] = 7/2, which is not a face of the die (Example 1.4).

front: Is Var(X) always equal to E[X^2]?
back: Hypothesis: finite probability space with positive weights. No. Var(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2 (Proposition 2.2), so the two agree only when E[X] = 0. For the die E[X^2] = 91/6 and Var(X) = 35/12 (Example 2.5).

front: Does a seeded sample mean equal the expectation?
back: No. A seeded die sample mean (seed 2026, n = 10000) is 3.469, against E[X] = 7/2. A sample mean is an estimate from one run.
basis: Lab 1 (SIMULATED), seed 2026

front: What is the standard deviation of the two-point loss of Example 1.5, in cents?
back: About 54486.24 cents, the square root of 2968750000 cents squared (Example 2.6).

front: On a finite probability space with positive weights, is E[(X - c)^2] smallest at c = E[X]?
back: Yes. Hypotheses: finite probability space with positive weights. For every real c, E[(X - c)^2] = Var(X) + (E[X] - c)^2 (Problem P2), so the minimum is at c = E[X].

front: In Lab 1's seed-2027 loss sample of 10000 draws, how many draws give a loss of 250000 cents?
back: 489, against an expected count of 500. This is one run, and it gives no spread of the count.

front: What is the k-th moment of X?
back: E[X^k], for a positive integer k (Section 1).

front: What is the k-th central moment of X?
back: m_k = E[(X - mu)^k], with mu = E[X] (Section 1).

front: What is the first central moment m_1 of X?
back: Hypothesis: finite probability space with positive weights. m_1 = 0 (Proposition 1.1).

front: What is the second central moment m_2 of X?
back: Hypothesis: finite probability space with positive weights. m_2 = Var(X) (Proposition 1.1).

front: What is the standardized variable Z of X?
back: Hypotheses: finite probability space with positive weights, and X takes at least two values. Z = (X - mu)/sigma with sigma = sqrt(Var(X)) > 0 (Definition 2.1).

front: What is the skewness of X?
back: gamma_3 = E[Z^3], the third standardized moment, with Z = (X - mu)/sigma (Definitions 2.1 and 2.2).

front: What is the kurtosis of X?
back: gamma_4 = E[Z^4], the fourth standardized moment, with no subtraction of 3 (Definition 2.2).

front: How is the skewness written in central moments?
back: Hypotheses: at least two values, positive weights. gamma_3 = m_3/sigma^3 (Proposition 2.3).

front: How is the kurtosis written in central moments?
back: Hypotheses: at least two values, positive weights. gamma_4 = m_4/sigma^4 = m_4/m_2^2 (Proposition 2.3).

front: How does kurtosis change under Y = aX + b with a not zero?
back: Hypotheses: finite probability space with positive weights, X takes at least two values, and a is not 0. Kurtosis is unchanged (Proposition 2.4).

front: What is the lower bound on kurtosis, and when is it attained?
back: Hypotheses: at least two values, positive weights. gamma_4 >= 1, with equality if and only if X takes exactly two values, each with probability 1/2 (Proposition 2.5).

front: What is the skewness of a Bernoulli law with P(X = 1) = p?
back: With q = 1 - p and 0 < p < 1: gamma_3 = (1 - 2p)/sqrt(pq) (Example 2.6).

front: What is the kurtosis of a Bernoulli law with P(X = 1) = p?
back: With q = 1 - p and 0 < p < 1: gamma_4 = (1 - 3pq)/(pq) (Example 2.6).

front: What is the mean of the law on 0, 1, 2 and 10 with probabilities 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 and 1/8?
back: 7/4 (Section 3).

front: What is the variance of the law on 0, 1, 2 and 10 with probabilities 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 and 1/8?
back: Var(X) = m_2 = 163/16 (Section 3).

front: What is the kurtosis of the law on -2, 1, 3 with probabilities 2/5, 1/2, 1/10?
back: 5/3, from mean 0, m_2 = 3 and m_4 = 15 (Section 4).

front: Does a skewness of zero mean the law is symmetric?
back: No. The law on -2, 1, 3 with probabilities 2/5, 1/2, 1/10 has gamma_3 = 0 and is not symmetric about its mean (Section 4).

front: Is the kurtosis of every law equal to 3?
back: No. The Bernoulli law with p = 1/10 has gamma_4 = 73/9, and p = 1/4 gives gamma_4 = 7/3 (Example 2.6).

front: What sample skewness does the seed-2026 sample of 20000 draws give for the law on 0, 1, 2 and 10 with probabilities 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 and 1/8?
back: Skewness 2.065, against exact skewness 2.073 for the same law (Lab 1).
basis: Lab 1 (SIMULATED), seed 2026

front: What is the squared skewness of the Bernoulli law with p = 1/10?
back: 64/9, from (1 - 2p)^2/(pq) with pq = 9/100 (Example 2.6).

front: What is a joint table for X and Y?
back: A list of values p(x,y) >= 0 over pairs of values, with total 1 (Definition 1.1).

front: When are two events independent?
back: When P(A and B) = P(A) P(B) (Definition 1.2).

front: When are discrete random variables X and Y independent?
back: When p(x,y) = P(X = x) P(Y = y) for every pair (x,y) of values, so every cell of the joint table is the product of its two marginals (Definition 1.2).

front: Is the independence test applied cell by cell?
back: Yes. One cell that fails the product rule makes the pair dependent (Remark 1.3).

front: Are two events with positive probability and no common outcome independent?
back: No. Their intersection has probability 0, while P(A) P(B) > 0, so they are dependent (Proposition 1.4).

front: What is E[XY] for independent variables with finitely many values?
back: E[XY] = E[X] E[Y] (Proposition 1.5).

front: What is the covariance of X and Y?
back: Cov(X,Y) = E[(X - E[X])(Y - E[Y])] (Definition 1.6).

front: What is the shortcut formula for covariance?
back: Hypothesis: finitely many values. Cov(X,Y) = E[XY] - E[X] E[Y] (Proposition 1.7).

front: Do independent variables with finitely many values have zero covariance?
back: Yes, Cov(X,Y) = 0 (Proposition 1.8).

front: Does zero covariance imply independence?
back: No. For X uniform on {-1, 0, 1} and Y = X^2, the covariance is 0, but p(0,0) = 1/3 while P(X = 0) P(Y = 0) = 1/9 (Example 1.9).

front: What are the conditional distribution and the conditional expectation of X given Y = y, in the elementary form?
back: For P(Y = y) > 0: P(X = x | Y = y) = p(x,y)/P(Y = y), and E[X | Y = y] = sum over x of x P(X = x | Y = y) (Definition 2.1). Only finite tables are covered (Remark 2.2).

front: Does total expectation hold for a finite table?
back: Yes, for X and Y with finitely many values: E[X] = sum over y with P(Y = y) > 0 of E[X | Y = y] P(Y = y) (Proposition 2.3).

front: Under independence, does E[X | Y = y] equal E[X]?
back: Yes, when X and Y are independent with finitely many values: E[X | Y = y] = E[X] for every y with P(Y = y) > 0 (Proposition 2.4).

front: For the dependent table of Example 2.5, what is E[X | Y = 0]?
Do the marginals of a joint table decide whether X and Y are independent?
back: No. X and Y each take 0 and 1 with probability 1/2. Set p(0,0) = p(1,1) = 1/2 and p(0,1) = p(1,0) = 0. The marginals are those of independence, but p(0,0) = 1/2 differs from P(X = 0) P(Y = 0) = 1/4 (Section 3).

front: In Problem P3, what is Cov(1_A, 1_B) for disjoint events A and B with P(A) = a > 0 and P(B) = b > 0?
back: -ab (Problem P3): E[XY] = 0, while E[X] E[Y] = ab.

front: What is the standard deviation of X?
back: sigma_X = sqrt(Var(X)), the nonnegative square root of the variance (Lesson 2, Definition 2.1).

front: What is the correlation of X and Y?
back: rho(X,Y) = Cov(X,Y)/(sigma_X sigma_Y), defined when both standard deviations are positive. A constant has no correlation (Definition 1.4).

front: Is covariance symmetric in its two arguments?
back: Yes. Hypothesis: finitely many values. Cov(X,Y) = Cov(Y,X) (Proposition 1.1).

front: How does covariance scale?
back: Hypothesis: finitely many values. Cov(aX + b, cY + d) = ac Cov(X,Y) for real a, b, c and d (Proposition 1.2).

front: What bound does Cauchy-Schwarz give for covariance and correlation?
back: Hypothesis: finitely many values. Cov(X,Y)^2 <= Var(X) Var(Y). So when both standard deviations are positive, -1 <= rho <= 1 (Proposition 1.5).

front: Is correlation unchanged by positive affine maps?
back: Yes, when sigma_X > 0 and sigma_Y > 0. For a, c > 0 and any b and d, rho(aX + b, cY + d) = rho(X,Y) (Proposition 1.6).

front: What is the correlation of X and Y = aX + b when a > 0 and sigma_X > 0?
back: 1 (Example 1.7): Cov(X,Y) = a Var(X) and sigma_Y = a sigma_X.

front: For X uniform on {-1, 0, 1} and Y = X^2, what is Var(Y)?
What is the covariance matrix of a vector X of random variables X_1 to X_n?
back: The n by n matrix with entries Sigma_ij = Cov(X_i, X_j). Its diagonal entries are the variances (Definition 2.1).

front: What does it mean for a real symmetric matrix M to be positive semidefinite?
back: w^T M w >= 0 for every vector w (Definition 2.2).

front: Is every covariance matrix positive semidefinite?
back: Yes. A covariance matrix is symmetric, and w^T Sigma w = Var(sum of w_i X_i) >= 0 for every w (Proposition 2.3). The hypothesis is finitely many values.

front: What bounds hold for the entries of a covariance matrix?
back: Hypothesis: X has finitely many values. Every diagonal entry is nonnegative, and Sigma_ij^2 <= Sigma_ii Sigma_jj for all i and j (Proposition 2.4).

front: Does zero correlation mean the two variables are unrelated?
back: No. Remark 1.8 gives Y = X^2 with X uniform on {-1, 0, 1}: the correlation is 0 while Y is a function of X. Correlation measures linear association.

front: Is covariance unit-free, like correlation?
back: No. Cov(100X, 100Y) = 10^4 Cov(X,Y) (Proposition 1.2), while the correlation is unchanged by the same scaling when both standard deviations are positive (Proposition 1.6).

front: Is any symmetric matrix with positive diagonal entries a covariance matrix?
back: No. The matrix [[1, 2], [2, 1]] is symmetric with positive diagonal, but for a vector with finitely many values Proposition 2.4 needs 4 <= 1, which is false.

front: What is the normal distribution N(mu, sigma^2)?
back: The law with density exp(-(x - mu)^2/(2 sigma^2))/(sigma sqrt(2 pi)) on the real line, for sigma > 0 (Definition 1.1).

front: What is the standard normal law?
back: N(0,1), with density phi(z) = e^(-z^2/2)/sqrt(2 pi). A variable with this law is a standard normal variable (Definition 1.1).

front: What is the value of the Gaussian integral?
back: The integral of e^(-x^2/2) over the real line equals sqrt(2 pi) (Proposition 1.2). Under Assumption 1.

front: Is the normal density a probability density?
back: Yes. For sigma > 0 and real mu, the density is nonnegative and integrates to 1 (Proposition 1.3). Under Assumption 1.

front: What does standardization give for a normal variable?
back: If X ~ N(mu, sigma^2) with sigma > 0, then (X - mu)/sigma has the law N(0,1). Conversely, if Z is standard normal, then mu + sigma Z has the law N(mu, sigma^2) (Proposition 1.4). Under Assumption 1.

front: What is E[Z^2] for a standard normal variable Z?
back: 1, so Var(Z) = 1 (Proposition 1.5, by integration by parts). Under Assumption 1.

front: What is a chi-square variable with nu degrees of freedom?
back: W_nu = the sum of Z_i^2 for i = 1 to nu, for independent standard normal Z_i, with nu a positive integer (Definition 2.1).

front: What Laplace-transform identity does Lemma 2.3 give for a squared normal?
back: For s >= 0, E[e^(-s Z^2)] = (1 + 2s)^(-1/2) for a standard normal Z. Under Assumption 1 (Lemma 2.3).

front: What is E[1/W] for a chi-square variable W with nu degrees of freedom?
back: Hypothesis: nu a positive integer. If nu > 2, E[1/W] = 1/(nu - 2). If nu <= 2, E[1/W] is infinite (Proposition 2.4). Under Assumption 1.

front: What is the Student-t distribution with nu degrees of freedom?
back: The law of t = Z / sqrt(W/nu), with Z standard normal and W chi-square with nu degrees of freedom, independent of Z. Only positive integer nu is covered (Definition 2.5).

front: What is the mean of the Student-t with nu > 2 degrees of freedom?
back: 0 (Proposition 2.6). Hypothesis: nu a positive integer. Under Assumption 1.

front: What is Var(t_5)?
back: 5/3, from nu/(nu - 2) with nu = 5 (Proposition 2.6). Under Assumption 1.

front: Does a Student-t variable have variance 1 because it is standardized?
back: No. A Student-t with nu > 2 degrees of freedom has mean 0 and variance nu/(nu - 2), not 1 (Proposition 2.6). Under Assumption 1.

front: Does every Student-t have a finite variance, as every normal does?
back: No. For nu <= 2, E[t^2] = nu E[1/W] is infinite (Proposition 2.6). Under Assumption 1.

front: Can the variance of N(mu, sigma^2) be set separately from its mean?
back: No. Both parameters are determined by the law: E[X] = mu and Var(X) = sigma^2 (Proposition 1.5). Under Assumption 1.

front: In Lab 1 Part A, what is the sample variance of t at nu = 5, against 5/3?
back: 1.669114 against the formula 1.666667. The relative error 0.001469 uses unrounded values (n = 100000 seeded draws).

front: What is the moment-generating function of X, and what is its domain?
back: M_X(t) = E[e^(tX)] for each real t where this expectation is finite. The domain is the set of such t and always contains 0, where M_X(0) = 1 (Definition 1.1).

front: Is the moment-generating function of a finitely valued X finite for every real t?
back: Yes. Its domain is the whole real line (Proposition 1.2).

front: What is the moment-generating function of N(mu, sigma^2)?
back: exp(mu t + sigma^2 t^2/2) for every real t, for sigma > 0 (Proposition 1.3). Under Assumption 1.

front: What is the moment-generating function of the square of a standard normal?
back: E[e^(tZ^2)] = (1 - 2t)^(-1/2) for t < 1/2. The domain is (-infinity, 1/2) (Proposition 1.4). Under Assumption 1.

front: What is the complex exponential e^(ia)?
back: cos a + i sin a, with modulus 1 (Definition 2.1).

front: What is the characteristic function of X?
back: phi_X(t) = E[e^(itX)] for each real t (Definition 2.2).

front: What bounds the characteristic function of X?
back: Hypothesis: X has finitely many values or has a density (Assumption 1(c) in the density case). Then |phi_X(t)| <= 1 for every real t, and phi_X(0) = 1 (Proposition 2.3).

front: How does the characteristic function transform under Y = aX + b?
back: phi_(aX+b)(t) = e^(itb) phi_X(at) for every real t (Proposition 2.4).

front: What is the characteristic function of a two-point law with P(X = a) = p and P(X = b) = 1 - p, for 0 < p < 1?
back: phi_X(t) = p e^(ita) + (1 - p) e^(itb) (Proposition 2.5).

front: What is |phi_X(t)|^2 for a two-point law with P(X = a) = p and P(X = b) = 1 - p, for 0 < p < 1?
back: p^2 + (1 - p)^2 + 2p(1 - p) cos(t(a - b)) (Proposition 2.5).

front: What is the moment-generating function of a sum of independent finitely valued variables?
back: Hypothesis: X and Y independent with finitely many values. M_(X+Y)(t) = M_X(t) M_Y(t) for every real t (Problem P3).

front: Is the moment-generating function of every random variable finite for every real t?
back: No. For W = Z^2, E[e^(tW)] is infinite for t >= 1/2 (Proposition 1.4). Under Assumption 1.

front: Is the moment-generating function of a sum the sum of the two functions?
back: No. If X = Y, then M_(X+Y)(t) = M_X(2t), which is 1 at t = 0, while M_X(0) + M_Y(0) = 2.

front: Does the characteristic function exist only for a variable with a density?
back: No. It exists for every finitely valued variable (Proposition 2.3), and the two-point law of Proposition 2.5 has no density.

back: 7.11e-13, at t = 2 (closed form 244.69193226), for X ~ N(0.5, 1.5^2). This is a numerical quadrature result, not a simulation.

front: What is a standard normal vector of length k?
back: A vector Z of k coordinates Z_1 to Z_k that are independent, each with the standard normal law of Lesson 6.

front: What are the second moments of a standard normal vector?
back: E[Z_i Z_j] = 1 if i = j and 0 if i is not j. In matrix form E[ZZ^T] = I (Proposition 1.1), under Lesson 6's Assumption 1.

front: When is a random vector X multivariate normal with mean mu and covariance matrix Sigma?
back: When X has the same law as mu + AZ for some matrix A with AA^T = Sigma, where Z is a standard normal vector. A is a factor of Sigma (Definition 1.2).

front: What is the mean of X = mu + AZ?
back: E[X] = mu (Proposition 1.3), under Lesson 6's Assumption 1.

front: What is the covariance matrix of X = mu + AZ?
back: AA^T (Proposition 1.3), under Lesson 6's Assumption 1. It is not A^T A (Example 1.5).

front: Is the factor of a covariance matrix unique?
back: No. If QQ^T = I, then AQ is also a factor of AA^T and, under Lesson 6's Assumption 1, gives the same mean and covariance (Remark 1.4).

front: For A = [[2, 0], [1, 1]], what is AA^T?
back: [[4, 2], [2, 2]], which is Sigma (Example 1.5).

front: Is AA^T symmetric and nonnegative in the quadratic form sense?
back: Yes. For a real matrix A, (AA^T)^T = AA^T, and w^T AA^T w = |A^T w|^2 >= 0 for every w (Proposition 1.6).

front: Does a singular covariance matrix have an inverse?
back: No. If Sigma = AA^T is not positive definite, some nonzero w has Sigma w = 0, so Sigma has no inverse (Proposition 2.1).

front: Do normal margins determine the joint law?
back: No. X and Y = epsilon X are standard normal and uncorrelated, where epsilon = 1 or -1 with probability 1/2 each, independent of X. Yet P(X + Y = 0) >= 1/2, while X and an independent standard normal X' have P(X + X' = 0) = 0 (Section 4).

front: Is the matrix of Example 1.5 positive definite?
back: Yes. For Sigma = [[4, 2], [2, 2]], w^T Sigma w = (2w_1 + w_2)^2 + w_2^2, which is zero only when w = 0 (Problem P3, which evaluates A^T w for the factor of Example 1.5).

back: 0.0187, in the off-diagonal entries (n = 20000, one run).

front: What is Chebyshev's inequality?
back: Hypothesis: a finitely valued Y with mean m and variance v, and a > 0. Then P(|Y - m| >= a) <= v/a^2 (Proposition 1.1).

front: What is the mean of the sample mean?
back: E[Xbar_n] = mu. Hypotheses: identically distributed X_i with mean mu and variance sigma^2, where 0 < sigma^2 < infinity, and X_i and X_j independent for i not equal to j (Proposition 1.2).

front: What does the weak law of large numbers state?
back: Hypotheses: identically distributed X_i with mean mu and variance sigma^2, where 0 < sigma^2 < infinity, X_i and X_j independent for i not equal to j, and every law finitely valued. Then P(|Xbar_n - mu| >= eps) <= sigma^2/(n eps^2) for every eps > 0 and every n >= 1, so the probability tends to 0 (Theorem 1.3).

front: What does the law of large numbers mean?
back: For identically distributed variables with mean mu, P(|Xbar_n - mu| >= eps) tends to 0 as n grows, for every eps > 0 (Definition 1.4).

front: Which dependence hypothesis does the weak law's proof use?
back: Only pairwise independence, through the zero covariance E[(X_i - mu)(X_j - mu)] = 0 for i not equal to j (Proposition 1.2 and the text after Theorem 1.3).

front: What is the product rule for independent variables and their characteristic functions?
back: Hypotheses: X_1 to X_n finitely valued and independent. E[prod g_i(X_i)] = prod E[g_i(X_i)], so phi of the sum is the product of the phi_(X_i). For i.i.d. variables the product is phi_X(t)^n (Proposition 2.1).

front: What is the expansion of a characteristic function near zero?
back: Hypotheses: Y finitely valued with E[Y] = 0, E[Y^2] = 1, M = max|Y| > 0, and |s| <= 1/M. Then |phi_Y(s) - (1 - s^2/2)| <= |s|^3 E|Y|^3/3 (Proposition 2.2).

front: What are the mean and the second moment of the standardized sample mean Z_n?
back: E[Z_n] = 0 and E[Z_n^2] = 1 for every n. Hypotheses: i.i.d. variables with finitely many values and sigma^2 > 0 (Proposition 2.3(a)).

front: Is the central limit theorem's conclusion about distribution functions proved in Section 2?
back: No. Proposition 2.3(b) gives the characteristic-function limit under Assumption 1 of Section 2. The lesson states no result that turns that limit into convergence of distribution functions, and it does not identify e^(-t^2/2) with the characteristic function of the standard normal law (Problem R2).

front: What is the central limit theorem in the sense of Definition 2.4?
back: The CLT holds for X when P(Z_n <= z) tends to Phi(z) for every real z, where Phi is the standard normal distribution function (Definition 2.4).

front: Can the Chebyshev bound sigma^2/(n eps^2) exceed 1?
back: Yes, when n eps^2 < sigma^2, and then the bound says nothing about the probability. Problem M3 has n = 2, eps = 1/2 and sigma^2 = 1, where the bound is 2 (Problem M3).

front: Does the law of large numbers say the sample mean is close to mu at every n?
back: No. Theorem 1.3 bounds the probability of a large deviation at each n, and that bound tends to 0 only as n grows.

front: Does the central limit theorem mean the sample mean is normally distributed for large n?
back: No. The theorem concerns the standardized mean Z_n and its limit (Definition 2.4). A finitely valued sample mean has no normal law for any finite n (Section 3).

front: Does the central limit theorem need the variables themselves to be normal?
back: No. The statement needs i.i.d. copies with finite positive variance sigma^2, and normality of X is not one of its hypotheses (Section 4).

front: What is the Chebyshev bound on P(|Xbar_100 - 3.5| >= 0.5) for the fair die?
back: 7/60, about 0.1167, from sigma^2/(n eps^2) with sigma^2 = 35/12 (Problem M1).

front: For ten fair dice, which integer threshold makes Z_10 <= 1 equivalent to S_10 <= threshold?
back: 40. The bound is 35 + sqrt(29.1667) = 40.4006, and S_10 is an integer, so S_10 <= 40 (Problem E1).

back: 0.8552, with standard error 0.0056, from 4000 seeded replications.

front: What is a heavy-tailed random variable?
back: X is heavy-tailed when e^(cx) P(|X| > x) tends to infinity as x grows, for every c > 0 (Definition 1.1).

front: What is the density of the standard Cauchy law?
back: 1/(pi(1 + x^2)) (Definition 1.2).

front: What is the distribution function of the standard Cauchy law?
back: F_C(x) = 1/2 + (1/pi) arctan x, under Assumption 2 (Proposition 1.3).

front: What is the distribution function of the t(3) law?
back: F_V(x) = 1/2 + (1/pi)(arctan(x/sqrt 3) + (x/sqrt 3)/(1 + x^2/3)), under Assumptions 1 and 2 (Proposition 1.3).

front: What is P(|C| > x) for the standard Cauchy law and x > 0?
back: (2/pi) arctan(1/x), under Assumption 2 (Proposition 1.4).

front: What is P(|V| > x) for the t(3) law and x > 0?
back: (2/pi)(arctan(sqrt 3/x) - x sqrt 3/(3 + x^2)), under Assumptions 1 and 2 (Proposition 1.4).

front: Is the standard Cauchy law heavy-tailed?
back: Yes, under Assumption 2 (Proposition 1.5(a)).

front: Is the Student-t law with 3 degrees of freedom heavy-tailed?
back: Yes, under Assumption 1 (Proposition 1.5(b)).

front: What is the limit of x P(|C| > x) as x grows?
back: 2/pi, under Assumption 2 (Proposition 1.7).

front: Does the standard Cauchy law have a finite variance?
back: No. E[C^2] is infinite, because x^2 >= |x| for |x| >= 1 and E|C| is infinite (Proposition 2.1).

front: What is the variance of the t(3) law?
back: 3, cited from Lesson 6 as nu/(nu - 2) at nu = 3 under Lesson 6's Assumption 1. It is not derived here (Remark 2.2).

front: Is the fourth moment of the t(3) law finite?
back: No. E[V^4] is infinite, so the kurtosis of Lesson 3 is not defined for V (Proposition 2.3). Under Assumption 1.

front: What is the failure of the CLT under infinite variance?
back: The situation in which Var(X) is not finite. The standardization of Lesson 9 then has no finite sigma, so the normal limit of Lesson 9 is not established for it (Definition 2.4).

front: Does a heavy tail mean large values occur often?
back: Not by itself. A heavy tail describes the decay of P(|X| > x) as x grows (Definition 1.1), not the size of one tail probability. For the Cauchy law at x = 10, P(|C| > 10) = (2/pi) arctan(0.1) = 0.063451 under Assumption 2, about 1 draw in 16, against 1.5240 x 10^-23 for the normal.

front: Does averaging always reduce the spread of a sample mean by the factor sqrt(n)?
back: No. The sqrt(n) scaling is Lesson 9's result for finite variance, and the Cauchy law has no finite variance (Proposition 2.1).

front: Does the Cauchy law have mean 0 by symmetry, so that the sample mean estimates 0?
back: No. Symmetry does not give a mean when the integral does not converge absolutely. E|C| is infinite (Proposition 2.1), so E[C] is not defined.

front: What are the quartiles of the standard Cauchy law, and what is their difference?
back: -1 and 1, from F_C(q) = 1/4 and 3/4 under Assumption 2, so the interquartile range is 2 (Problem P2).

front: What does x P(|C| > x) equal at x = 10 in Lab 1 Part D, and how does it compare with 2/pi?
back: 0.634510, from (2/pi) arctan(0.1) times 10 under Assumption 2. The limit is 2/pi, about 0.636620, so the value at x = 10 is about 0.002 below it (Problem E1).

front: What is the infimum of a set A of real numbers that is bounded below?
back: inf A is the greatest real number that is at most every member of A (Section 3).

front: When are variables X and Y independent in Remark 2.2?
back: When P(X in A, Y in B) = P(X in A) P(Y in B) for all sets A and B (Remark 2.2).

front: When is a symmetric matrix M positive definite?
back: When w^T M w > 0 for every nonzero vector w (Section 1, after Proposition 1.6).

front: What is the sample covariance matrix with divisor n - 1?
back: For draws X^(1) to X^(n) of a random vector, its (r, s) entry is the sum over t of (X_r^(t) - Xbar_r)(X_s^(t) - Xbar_s), divided by n - 1, where Xbar_r is the sample mean of coordinate r (Section 3).

front: What does it mean for the variables of the sample mean to be identically distributed?
back: Each X_i has the same law as one variable X, with mean mu and variance sigma^2, where 0 < sigma^2 < infinity (Section 1).

front: What is the sample mean Xbar_n of the first n variables?
back: The sum of the first n variables divided by n (Section 1).

front: What does i.i.d. mean for the variables of Section 2?
back: Independent and identically distributed: the joint probability of any tuple of values factorizes into the product of the one-variable probabilities, and each X_i has the law of X (Section 2).

front: What is a light-tailed law?
back: A law that is not heavy-tailed (Section 1, after Definition 1.1).

front: What is the standard deviation of a fair six-sided die?
back: sqrt(35/12), about 1.708 (Example 2.5).

front: What covariance matrix does the two-asset construction X1 = S1 Z1, X2 = S2(rho Z1 + sqrt(1 - rho^2) Z2) have?
back: [[S1^2, rho S1 S2], [rho S1 S2, S2^2]]. Under the hypotheses of Example 2.5 (S1, S2 > 0; |rho| < 1; Z1, Z2 independent with mean 0 and variance 1), and assuming its Assumption 1, that the rules of Proposition 1.1 hold for Z1 and Z2 (not proved here).

front: For the table of Example 3.6, for which p is Q(p) = 1?
back: Hypotheses: positive weights and distinct values. Exactly for p in (3/5, 4/5], because F(0) = 3/5 < p <= F(1) = 4/5 (Proposition 3.2; Example 3.6).

front: How is the probability P(A) of an event A defined on a finite probability space?
back: P(A) is the sum of p(omega) over the outcomes omega in A (Section 1).

front: What is the support of a random variable X?
back: The set of values that X takes on Omega. A value x is in the support exactly when P(X = x) > 0 (Definition 1.2).

front: For a finite law with positive weights and distinct values x_1 to x_m in increasing order, what is F(x) for x_k <= x < x_(k+1)?
back: Hypotheses: positive weights and distinct values. F(x) = F_k, where F_k is the sum of the first k weights p_1 to p_k, for 1 <= k < m (Proposition 2.2(b)-(c)).

front: Is the distribution function of a finite law right-continuous at each value?
back: Yes. Hypotheses: positive weights and distinct values. F is right-continuous at each value x_k (Proposition 2.2(d)).

front: Is the quantile function of a finite law left-continuous on (0, 1]?
back: Yes. Hypotheses: positive weights and distinct values. If u_n increases to p, then Q(u_n) tends to Q(p) (Remark 3.3).

front: What is Var(X) for a fair six-sided die?
back: Hypothesis: finite probability space with positive weights. 35/12, from E[X^2] = 91/6 and E[X] = 7/2, by Proposition 2.2 (Example 2.5).

front: In which units is the standard deviation of X measured?
back: In the units of X. sigma = sqrt(Var(X)) is in the units of X, while Var(X) is in squared units (Definition 2.1).

front: What is the third central moment of the law on 0, 1, 2 and 10 with probabilities 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 and 1/8?
What is the fourth central moment of the law on 0, 1, 2 and 10 with probabilities 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 and 1/8?
What are the marginal probabilities P(X = x) and P(Y = y) in a joint table for X and Y?
back: P(X = x) = sum over y of p(x,y), and P(Y = y) = sum over x of p(x,y) (Definition 1.1).

front: Can conditional expectations be equal for every y while the pair is dependent?
back: Yes. For Y = X^2 with X uniform on {-1, 0, 1}, E[X | Y = 0] = E[X | Y = 1] = E[X] = 0, yet the pair is dependent (Problem R3).

front: What is E[Z] for a standard normal variable Z?
back: 0, because z phi(z) is odd (Proposition 1.5). Under Assumption 1.

front: For A = [[2, 0], [1, 1]], what is A^T A?
back: [[5, 1], [1, 1]], which differs from Sigma (Example 1.5).

front: For A = [[2, 0], [1, 1]] and Q = [[0, -1], [1, 0]], what is the second factor B = AQ?
What is the density of the Student-t law with 3 degrees of freedom?
back: 2/(pi sqrt 3)(1 + t^2/3)^(-2), the law of Lesson 6 at nu = 3, taken as Assumption 1 (Definition 1.2).

front: Is covariance additive in its first argument?
back: Yes. Hypothesis: finitely many values. Cov(X + Z, Y) = Cov(X,Y) + Cov(Z,Y) (Proposition 1.1).

front: When is a law symmetric about its mean?
back: When X - mu and -(X - mu) have the same distribution. This is a statement about the whole law, not about one moment (Section 4).

front: What is the mean of the standardized variable Z?
back: E[Z] = 0. Hypotheses: X takes at least two values, with positive weights (Proposition 2.3).

front: What is the variance of the standardized variable Z?
back: Var(Z) = 1. Hypotheses: X takes at least two values, with positive weights (Proposition 2.3).

front: How does skewness change under Y = aX + b with a not zero?
back: Hypotheses: finite probability space with positive weights, X takes at least two values, and a is not 0. Skewness is multiplied by sign(a) (Proposition 2.4). So Y = -X has the opposite skewness: reversing the sign of X does not leave it unchanged.

front: What integral gives E[1/W] for a chi-square variable W with nu degrees of freedom?
back: E[1/W] = the integral from 0 to infinity of (1 + 2s)^(-nu/2) ds, a value in (0, infinity] (Lemma 2.3). Under Assumption 1.

front: What is the variance of the sample mean?
back: Var(Xbar_n) = sigma^2/n. Hypotheses: identically distributed X_i with mean mu and variance sigma^2, where 0 < sigma^2 < infinity, and X_i and X_j independent for i not equal to j (Proposition 1.2).

front: What is the limit of the characteristic function of the standardized sample mean Z_n?
back: phi_(Z_n)(t) tends to e^(-t^2/2) for every real t. Hypotheses: i.i.d. variables with finitely many values, and Assumption 1 of Section 2 (Proposition 2.3(b)).

front: Is the covariance of X with itself nonnegative?
